summary: This work demonstrates fast mid-circuit measurement and real-time feedforward in a neutral-atom array by coupling qubits to a high-finesse optical cavity, reducing measurement-and-feedforward cycle times from ~1 ms to below 100 μs. The approach uses site-selective light shifts to protect unmeasured data qubits and Purcell-enhanced photon collection from measured qubits, achieving sub-percent measurement infidelity with less than 2% coherence loss on unread qubits.
motivation: Neutral-atom arrays are a leading platform for quantum information, but their mid-circuit measurement speeds have been limited to >1 ms by the time needed for atom transport to measurement zones and free-space photodetection, slowing implementations of error correction, adaptive circuits, and measurement-based protocols by three orders of magnitude relative to coherent operations.
method: Five $^{87}$Rb atoms in a 1D tweezer array couple to a near-concentric Fabry–Perot cavity with cooperativity $C=3.0$ (single-photon Rabi frequency $g_0/2\pi=3.1$ MHz, cavity linewidth $\kappa/2\pi=0.53$ MHz, atomic linewidth $\gamma/2\pi=3.0$ MHz). Measured qubits are driven with a probe beam detuned $\Delta_{pa}=2\pi\times 10$ MHz from the $|F=2\rangle\to|F'=3\rangle$ transition and resonant with the cavity; unmeasured qubits are protected by infrared shielding beams inducing $\Delta_s$ shifts on excited states. An FPGA implements adaptive gating to stop the probe after two photons are detected and controls real-time feedforward microwave rotations.
result: Per-atom detection infidelities of $0.9^{+0.4}_{-0.3}$% (bright) and $0.2^{+0.4}_{-0.2}$% (dark) are achieved in 40 μs windows with 20 μs switching intervals; mid-circuit measurements of four qubits reduce coherence of a fifth data qubit by <2% (state-preserving fidelity $\mathcal{F}=100(2)$%). Adaptive feedforward reduces measurement-induced phase-shift slope from $0.020(2)$ rad/μs to $0.002(2)$ rad/μs, raising fidelity from 96(2)% to 99(2)%. Quantum-state discrimination and coherent state preparation succeed with 81(2)% and 85(2)% probability respectively using adaptive measurements, compared to 69–73% and 72–78% for fixed-axis schemes; total cycle time is 45 μs per qubit.
